clue.text: Urge to go into action, though dispirited

indicators.note: going into something means entering it, so the urge ends up enclosed by the action

blocks.note: to urge someone is to press them
a deed is an action

explanation.surface: Someone feels pushed into doing something even while their spirits are low.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for action is split by the urge, so its first two letters stand before the insert and its last two after.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a person low in mood, sad and lacking energy or hope.

clue.text: Got out of doing something

blocks.note: surface reading: avoided a task, dodged a chore
setter's reading: obtained as the result of doing work

explanation.walkthrough: 'Got out of' suggests escaping work, but here it means gained from it.
explanation.definitionFit: Money or credit gained through work or effort is what is deserved and received for labour.

clue.text: Gold goes up when two firms are after it for decoration

definitions.note: noun for a style of decoration; the answer usually names the ornate style

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the word is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: or is gold in heraldry
CO is the abbreviation for company, twice

explanation.surface: The gold price rises when two companies chase it to make ornaments.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'goes up' turns the gold word upwards; the firms follow it.
explanation.definitionFit: Rococo is the elaborate eighteenth-century ornamental style, full of scrolls and shell motifs.

clue.text: Banger unfortunately overturned on motorway

indicators.note: something overturned is upside down, so in a down entry the word is written in reverse

blocks.note: alas expresses regret, like unfortunately
the M1 motorway, read as MI

explanation.surface: A car crash: an old banger has flipped over on the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: A banger is British slang for a sausage, and also for an old car, which the surface uses.
explanation.definitionFit: Salami is a type of cured sausage, and banger is British slang for a sausage.

clue.text: Determined, though certain to come in last

indicators.note: coming in means entering, so the word for certain goes inside the other

blocks.note: the last part of anything is its end
sure means certain

explanation.surface: A runner is determined, even though sure to finish last.
explanation.definitionFit: To have ensured something is to have made certain of it, settling or determining the outcome.

clue.text: Trying to write with such a pencil would be

definitions.text: Trying to write with such a pencil would be

blocks.note: surface reading: a pencil with no sharpened tip

blocks.clueFragment: Trying to write with such a pencil would be
blocks.note: setter's reading: the attempt would be futile, the word describing both the blunt pencil and the effort

explanation.walkthrough: The one word describes the blunt pencil literally and the effort figuratively.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means futile or useless, and literally describes a pencil whose tip has broken off.

clue.text: Now for a West End gift

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the final letter of the word
a present is a gift

explanation.surface: Something to give as a present right now in London's West End shops.
explanation.walkthrough: The West End is London's theatre and shopping district, but here the phrase means the end of West.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means currently, at this moment in time, which is the sense of the adverb.

clue.text: Sailor on boat - he used to work with ropes

definitions.text: he used to work with ropes

blocks.note: Jack is a traditional name for a sailor, as in Jack Tar
a ketch is a two-masted sailing boat

explanation.surface: A sailor aboard a boat, an old hand at handling the rigging.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the sailor above the boat. Jack Ketch was a notorious seventeenth-century English hangman.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack Ketch was a London executioner whose name became a byword for the hangman, who worked with the noose.

clue.text: Barmaid who argued about a pound

definitions.text: Barmaid who argued about a pound

blocks.note: surface reading: a woman who serves drinks in a pub

blocks.clueFragment: Barmaid who argued about a pound
blocks.note: setter's reading: a maid of the legal bar, the Shakespeare heroine who disguised herself as a lawyer and argued over a pound of flesh

explanation.surface: A pub barmaid quarrels with a customer over a pound in change.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Merchant of Venice, Portia poses as a lawyer and defeats Shylock's claim to a pound of Antonio's flesh; the bar here is the legal profession, not a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's heroine acts as advocate in court, a woman at the legal bar, and her case concerns Shylock's bond of flesh.

clue.text: Charge sheet?

blocks.note: surface reading: the police record of the offence someone is accused of
setter's reading: a sheet showing what a shop charges for each item

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that charge means cost, not a criminal accusation.
explanation.definitionFit: A document listing what goods cost is literally a sheet of charges made to customers.

clue.text: Protection worn by king hiding in a tree

indicators.note: something hiding in a place is tucked inside it, so the king goes within the tree

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for king (Latin rex)
an oak is a tree

explanation.surface: A king, like Charles II after Worcester, shelters in an oak tree for protection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a tree' is read as AN OAK, with R tucked inside after the O.
explanation.definitionFit: An anorak is a waterproof hooded jacket, worn as protection against wind and rain.

clue.text: Criterion for judges to observe?

blocks.note: the bench is the collective term for judges or magistrates
to mark something is to notice or observe it

explanation.surface: A question about what standard judges should follow when they observe proceedings.
explanation.definitionFit: A benchmark is a standard or reference point against which other things are measured or judged.

clue.text: Rarely seen part of the French President's residence

indicators.note: only a part of the preceding words is wanted, a run of letters spanning them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word into the second

explanation.surface: A remark about a room of the Paris presidential palace that visitors seldom get to see.
explanation.definitionFit: The Elysee Palace in Paris is the official home and office of France's head of state.

clue.text: It reduces glare from headlamps

indicators.note: the answer is made from the letters of the next word, rebuilt into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Something that cuts down the dazzle of car headlights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' signals that the answer is made out of the letters of the final word.
explanation.definitionFit: A shade over a light bulb softens and diffuses the light, cutting down harsh brightness in a room.

clue.text: Papal bull's counterpart that's beyond criticism

blocks.note: surface reading: a decree issued by the Pope, and its equivalent
setter's reading: a holy male bovine, whose female counterpart is a holy one too

explanation.walkthrough: A papal bull is a formal decree from the Pope; read literally it is a holy bull, whose female counterpart is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes an institution or idea treated as immune from questioning or attack.

clue.text: Weak team member transferred by coach, perhaps

blocks.note: first meaning: someone carried along by colleagues without contributing
second meaning: someone carried on a vehicle as a traveller

explanation.surface: A poor player gets transferred by the team's coach to another club.
explanation.walkthrough: Coach suggests a sports trainer moving a player, but it is the bus.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a traveller carried in a vehicle, and figuratively a member who contributes little and is carried by others.

clue.text: Fuss after a party

blocks.note: taken as written
a do is an informal word for a party

explanation.surface: The commotion that follows a celebration.
explanation.definitionFit: Ado means bustle or trouble, as in much ado about nothing, so it is a fuss.

clue.text: Took down a note

blocks.note: taken as written
te is a note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: Someone wrote down a note, as in dictation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Took down' looks like writing a note, but it means swallowed.
explanation.definitionFit: To take food down is to swallow it, which is what eating means.

clue.text: Changes to a cereal

indicators.note: making changes to the following letters means rearranging them into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone switches over to a different breakfast cereal.
explanation.definitionFit: The oat is a cereal grass grown for its grain, used in porridge and oatmeal.

clue.text: Girl meets chap and starts talking - but doesn't yield

definitions.note: verb phrase for an adjective: someone adamant does not yield

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, so only that letter is used

blocks.note: Ada is a girl's name
a chap is a man
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A girl meets a man and begins chatting, but she refuses to give in to him.
explanation.definitionFit: Adamant means unshakeably firm in a decision, the attitude of someone who refuses to give way.

clue.text: Poison scare in new development

indicators.note: a new development of the letters is a fresh arrangement of them

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A news report of a fresh poisoning alarm.
explanation.definitionFit: Arsenic is a chemical element whose compounds are notorious toxins, the classic murder weapon of detective fiction.

clue.text: Creature with pointed small feet

blocks.note: given a point of the compass, here east
FT is the short form of feet

explanation.surface: An animal described as having sharp little feet.
explanation.walkthrough: E for east is one of the four compass points, so 'pointed' means a point is supplied.
explanation.definitionFit: An eft is a newt, especially a young one, a small amphibian creature.

clue.text: It comes from a conifer, naturally

definitions.text: It comes from a conifer, naturally

indicators.note: read as in a natural or untamed way, the letters of the tree are let loose and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Something that grows on an evergreen tree as a matter of course.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition, while 'naturally' also tells you to rework the tree's letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The woody seed-bearing structure of a fir tree grows on that evergreen, so it naturally comes from one.

clue.text: The land of the living?

blocks.note: surface reading: the world of those still alive, as opposed to the dead
setter's reading: a living is a church benefice, and this is the district a vicar's living covers

explanation.walkthrough: In the Church of England a vicar's post and income is called a living, and it comes with a defined area of land and people.
explanation.definitionFit: A parish is the territory served by one clergyman, whose appointment is known as his living.

clue.text: He wrote for various papers

indicators.note: various suggests something varied, so the letters are mixed into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A journalist who contributed to several newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: Sapper was the pen name of H. C. McNeile, creator of the Bulldog Drummond thrillers.
explanation.definitionFit: The pseudonym belonged to a British author of popular adventure novels, so he was a writer.

clue.text: Raise drink after drink: result - uproar!

indicators.note: to raise is to lift up, and in a down entry a lifted word reads bottom to top

blocks.note: rum is a spirit, a drink
to sup is to drink

explanation.surface: A rowdy round of drinks, one after another, ends in a noisy row.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'Raise' lifts the first-written drink upward, and it is placed after the spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: A rumpus is a noisy disturbance or commotion, a synonym for uproar or row.

clue.text: Confused sunbather misses bus to capital

indicators.note: missing something means failing to have it, so those letters are left out
a confused arrangement is jumbled, so the remaining letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A sunbather, flustered, fails to catch the bus to the city.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters B, U and S are struck from the long word in any order, then the rest is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Tehran is the capital city of Iran, seat of its government.

clue.text: Walkabout certain to be rated highly

indicators.note: about means around, so the walking word is placed round the certain word

blocks.note: split as walk, a synonym of tread, with about acting as an instruction
sure means certain

explanation.surface: A royal walkabout is certain to win high praise.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's single word for a royal stroll among crowds has to be broken in two: the first half supplies letters and the second gives the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Something treasured is valued greatly and held dear, so it is rated highly.

clue.text: Beating the retreat

blocks.note: first meaning: a thrashing, as in giving someone a good one
second meaning: the state of being concealed, as in going into it

explanation.surface: A military phrase, beating the retreat, the drum signal for troops to withdraw.
explanation.walkthrough: Beating the retreat is a ceremonial drum display, but the clue splits into two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a physical thrashing and also concealment, a withdrawal to a secret place out of sight.

clue.text: Flattery works in this kind of TV

blocks.note: soft soap is flattery, shortened to soap
opera is the plural of opus, a work

explanation.surface: Flattering people is how you get on in television.
explanation.definitionFit: A soap opera is a long-running television serial drama about everyday lives, a particular genre of TV.

clue.text: His job is to transfer stock

definitions.text: His job is to transfer stock

blocks.note: surface reading: moving shares from one owner to another, a stockbroker's work

blocks.clueFragment: His job is to transfer stock
blocks.note: setter's reading: stock as livestock, herded from one place to another

explanation.definitionFit: A drover herds cattle or sheep over long distances to market or new pasture, moving livestock.

clue.text: Stand for soldier's award

blocks.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, so a soldier
to award something is to present it

explanation.surface: A soldier stands to receive a medal.
explanation.definitionFit: To represent is to symbolise or act on behalf of, which is what standing for something means.
